title: The Imitation of Christ
author: thomas-a-kempis
attributionNote: The Imitation is traditionally ascribed to Thomas à Kempis, an Augustinian canon of Mount St Agnes near Zwolle, and that attribution has been the majority view since the 15th century. Its authorship was disputed for centuries among the houses of the Devotio Moderna, and the question is still argued.
description: The Imitation of Christ is the most widely read devotional book in the Christian West: four books of short chapters on the interior life, the contempt of the world, the following of Christ and the sacrament of communion. Book I treats humility, temptation and self-knowledge; Book II the inward kingdom; Book III, the longest, is a dialogue between the soul and Christ on consolation, suffering and the love of the cross; Book IV prepares the reader for communion. Its sober, direct prose has kept it in print for six centuries.
historicalContext: Thomas à Kempis wrote within the Devotio Moderna, the movement of common-life piety that arose in the Low Countries around Geert Groote and the Brethren of the Common Life. William Benham's translation of 1886, printed in London with an introductory note, is the version the archive carries.
availabilityNote: Complete. All four books — 115 chapters with the devotional exhortation that opens Book IV — are streamed from the Internet Sacred Text Archive at read time, one printed chapter per chapter. Chapter labels carry the book they belong to, because the printed numbering restarts in each book. The edition's introductory note is not part of the work.
